claim: Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD) affects 12/100,000 people.
source: Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD) is a prevalent myopathy, affecting 12/100,000 people (Deenen et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Deenen et al., 2014

claim: Skeletal muscle weakness in FSHD often appears first in the facial and shoulder girdle muscles.
source: Although clinical severity is highly variable, skeletal muscle weakness often appears first in the facial and shoulder girdle muscles, with muscles of the trunk and lower extremities becoming affected as the disease progresses.
evidence: Supported by established clinical knowledge about FSHD presentation

claim: Distinctive features of FSHD include asymmetric skeletal muscle wasting and scapular winging.
source: Distinctive features of FSHD include asymmetric skeletal muscle wasting and scapular winging (Tawil, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tawil, 2008

claim: Myoblasts from FSHD patients show increased susceptibility to oxidative stress.
source: Analysis of myoblasts from FSHD patients has revealed direct functional impairments, including increased susceptibility to oxidative stress (Winokur et al., 2003a, 2003b; Celegato et al., 2006; Macaione et al., 2007; Barro et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published studies

claim: FSHD patient myoblasts show up-regulation of apoptotic markers.
source: up-regulation of apoptotic markers (Winokur et al., 2003a, 2003b; Sandri et al., 2001; Vanderplanck et al., 2011; Laoudj-Chenivesse et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published studies

claim: FSHD patient myoblasts show repression of MYOD and MYOD-target genes.
source: repression of MYOD and MYOD-target genes (Winokur et al., 2003b; Celegato et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: Myogenic differentiation in FSHD results in myotubes with either an atrophic, or hypertrophic and highly disorganised morphology.
source: Additionally, myogenic differentiation results in myotubes with either an atrophic, or hypertrophic and highly disorganised morphology (Barro et al., 2010; Vanderplanck et al., 2011; Tassin et al., 2012; Ansseau et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published studies

claim: Defects in myoblast function likely result in impaired muscle maintenance, directly contributing to clinical symptoms in FSHD.
source: Defects in myoblast function are likely to result in impaired muscle maintenance, directly contributing to clinical symptoms (Morgan and Zammit, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation and logical inference from myoblast defects

claim: FSHD1 (1A) is associated with the contraction of a macrosatellite repeat named D4Z4 in the subtelomeric region 4q35.
source: FSHD1 (1A) (OMIM #158900) is associated with the contraction of a macrosatellite repeat named D4Z4 in the subtelomeric region 4q35 (Tawil, 2008; van Deutekom et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: Each D4Z4 repeat unit contains an open reading frame for Double homeodomain protein 4 (DUX4).
source: Embedded within each 3.3 kb D4Z4 repeat unit is an open reading frame (ORF) for Double homeodomain protein 4 (DUX4), an intron-less retrogene (Dixit et al., 2007; Gabriëls et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: Contraction of D4Z4 units to between 1–10 is associated with de-repression of chromatin.
source: Contraction of D4Z4 units to between 1–10 is associated with de-repression of chromatin (van Deutekom et al., 1993; Zeng et al., 2009; de Greef et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: DUX4 mRNA transcript from the distal D4Z4 repeat is stabilised when contraction occurs on a permissive chromosomal 4qA haplotype containing a polyadenylation site within the flanking pLAM region.
source: If this occurs on a permissive chromosomal 4qA haplotype containing a polyadenylation site within the flanking pLAM region, DUX4 mRNA transcript from the distal D4Z4 repeat is stabilised and DUX4 protein translated (Dixit et al., 2007; Lemmers et al., 2010; Snider et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: In FSHD2, de-repression of the D4Z4 macrosatellite occurs despite the presence of >11 D4Z4 repeats.
source: In the rarer FSHD2 (1B) (OMIM #158901), de-repression of the D4Z4 macrosatellite occurs despite the presence of >11 D4Z4 repeats, but still requires the permissive 4qA haplotype containing the polyadenylation signal (de Greef et al., 2009, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: FSHD2 has been linked to mutations in the SMCHD1 gene.
source: FSHD2 has recently been linked to mutations in the Structural maintenance of chromosomes flexible hinge domain containing 1 (SMCHD1) gene, encoding a protein involved in DNA methylation (Lemmers et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lemmers et al., 2012

claim: Mutations in DNMT3B have been implicated in perturbed epigenetic regulation in FSHD.
source: Recently, mutations in DNA methyltransferase 3B (DNMT3B) have also been implicated in perturbed epigenetic regulation in FSHD (van den Boogaard et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to van den Boogaard et al., 2016

claim: Aberrant DUX4 expression underlies pathogenesis in both FSHD1 and FSHD2.
source: Taken together, the consensus is that aberrant DUX4 expression underlies pathogenesis in both FSHD1 and FSHD2 (Tawil et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tawil et al., 2014 and represents scientific consensus

claim: DUX4-fl is mainly expressed in germline cells.
source: Two main DUX4 mRNA transcripts can be derived from the ORF in a D4Z4 repeat: DUX4-fl (full length) mainly expressed in germline cells, and the alternatively spliced DUX4-s (short) transcript expressed in some somatic cells.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about DUX4 expression patterns

claim: FSHD skeletal muscle expresses DUX4-fl whereas this transcript is not usually found in healthy control muscle.
source: FSHD skeletal muscle expresses DUX4-fl whereas this transcript is not usually found in healthy control muscle (Snider et al., 2010), although very low levels have been reported in some studies (Jones et al., 2012; Tassin et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: Expression of DUX4 in myoblasts recapitulates the pathogenic phenotype of myoblasts from FSHD patients.
source: Expression of DUX4 in myoblasts recapitulates the pathogenic phenotype of myoblasts from FSHD patients (Vanderplanck et al., 2011; Yao et al., 2014; Mitsuhashi et al., 2013; Bosnakovski et al., 2008a; Knopp, 2011; Geng et al., 2012; Bosnakovski et al., 2014; Kowaljow et al., 2007; Wallace et al., 2011; Geng et al., 2011; Banerji et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published studies

claim: Suppression of DUX4 expression using siRNA or anti-sense oligonucleotides rescues the atrophic phenotype of FSHD myotubes in vitro.
source: Indeed, suppression of DUX4 expression using siRNA or anti-sense oligonucleotides rescues the atrophic phenotype of FSHD myotubes in vitro (Vanderplanck et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vanderplanck et al., 2011

claim: DUX4 is a potent transcription factor.
source: DUX4 is a potent transcription factor and analysis of DUX4-expressing myoblasts has revealed that major transcriptional pathways such as cell cycle regulation, glutathione redox metabolism, myogenic differentiation and Wnt signalling are disrupted (Bosnakovski et al., 2008a; Geng et al., 2012; Banerji et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies showing transcriptional effects

claim: DUX4 expression upregulates many germline and neural genes.
source: In addition, many germline and neural genes are upregulated (Banerji et al., 2015; Dandapat et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: DUX4 is at very low levels in FSHD biopsies.
source: However, DUX4 is at very low levels in FSHD biopsies (Tassin et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tassin et al., 2013

claim: The transcriptional landscape of genes altered by DUX4 is much more prominent in FSHD patient-derived material than DUX4 expression levels would suggest.
source: Despite this, we, and others, have shown that the transcriptional landscape of genes altered by DUX4 is much more prominent in FSHD patient-derived material (Yao et al., 2014; Banerji et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies including authors' own work

claim: There is a significant overlap between DUX4-expressing murine satellite cell-derived myoblasts and human FSHD muscle gene expression.
source: Comparing gene expression data from DUX4-expressing murine satellite cell-derived myoblasts to a meta-analysis of published microarrays from FSHD patient biopsies and primary cultures (Banerji et al., 2015), we revealed a significant overlap between DUX4-expressing murine satellite cell-derived myoblasts and human FSHD muscle (Knopp et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies including authors' own work

claim: The receptor tyrosine kinase RET is up-regulated in DUX4-expressing myoblasts.
source: We found that the receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) Rearranged during transfection (RET) is up-regulated in DUX4-expressing myoblasts (Banerji et al., 2015; Dandapat et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies including authors' own work

claim: RET is a transmembrane RTK containing 4 cadherin-like repeats, a cysteine-rich area, and a calcium-binding site on the extracellular region.
source: RET is a transmembrane RTK containing 4 cadherin-like repeats, a cysteine-rich area, a calcium-binding site on the extracellular region and several intracellular tyrosine kinase domains (Santoro et al., 2004; Airaksinen and Saarma, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations describing RET structure

claim: There are two main RET isoforms: RET9 and RET51.
source: There are two main RET isoforms; RET9 and RET51, alternatively spliced in the 3' region, resulting in an additional tyrosine at Y1096 on RET51 (Jain et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jain et al., 2006

claim: RET9 and RET51 are differentially expressed, regulated and have diverse roles in development and tissue homeostasis.
source: These two main RET isoforms are differentially expressed, regulated and have diverse roles in development and tissue homeostasis (Yoong et al., 2005; Tsui-Pierchala et al., 2002; Richardson et al., 2012; Jain et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published studies

claim: RET is activated by the secreted Glial cell-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF) family ligands (GFL): GDNF, neurturin (NRTN), artemin (ARTN) and persephin (PSPN).
source: RET is activated by the secreted Glial cell-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF) family ligands (GFL): GDNF, neurturin (NRTN), artemin (ARTN) and persephin (PSPN).
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about RET signaling

claim: GFLs bind with high affinity to one of four glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored co-receptors of the GDNF Family Receptor (GFRα) family.
source: GFLs bind with high affinity to one of four glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored co-receptors of the GDNF Family Receptor (GFRα) family.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about RET signaling mechanism

claim: GFL:GFRα complexes recruit two RET molecules, triggering RET dimerisation and trans-phosphorylation.
source: GFL:GFRα complexes then recruit two RET molecules, triggering RET dimerisation and trans-phosphorylation of the intracellular region of both molecules.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about RET activation mechanism

claim: RET activation leads to recruitment of adaptor proteins and activation of downstream signalling cascades such as MAPK, PI3/AKT, JAK/STAT, JNK, ERK5, SRC and PLCγ.
source: This leads to recruitment of adaptor proteins and activation of downstream signalling cascades such as MAPK, PI3/AKT, JAK/STAT, JNK, ERK5, SRC and PLCγ (Santoro et al., 2004; Airaksinen and Saarma, 2002; Runeberg-Roos and Saarma, 2007; Mulligan, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: RET9 and RET51 activate PI3K/AKT and ERK signalling with different dynamics.
source: RET9 and RET51 activate PI3K/AKT and ERK signalling with different dynamics and have distinct abilities to recruit Src or Frs2, suggesting differential activation of downstream targets by the two main RET isoforms (Tsui-Pierchala et al., 2002; Ishiguro et al., 1999; Besset et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: Coordinated RET signalling is crucial for development of multiple tissues, including many neuronal cell types, kidneys and the thyroid gland.
source: Coordinated RET signalling is crucial for development of multiple tissues, including many neuronal cell types, kidneys and the thyroid gland (Runeberg-Roos and Saarma, 2007; Arighi et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: RET knockout mice can be embryonic lethal with a wide range of organ defects.
source: Indeed, RET knockout mice can be embryonic lethal with a wide range of organ defects (Jain et al., 2010; Schuchardt et al., 1994; de Graaff et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: RET signalling regulates spermatogonial and haematopoietic stem cell function.
source: RET signalling has also been shown to regulate spermatogonial and haematopoietic stem cell function (Naughton et al., 2006; Fonseca-Pereira et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: Inactivating mutations of RET lead to Hirschsprung's disease.
source: Dysregulated RET signalling is associated with disease: inactivating mutations of RET lead to a form of neurocristopathy called Hirschsprung's disease (Amiel et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to Amiel et al., 2008

claim: Mutations of RET resulting in constitutively active isoforms are associated with several forms of inherited and somatic cancers.
source: whereas mutations of RET resulting in constitutively active isoforms are associated with several forms of inherited and somatic cancers (Arighi et al., 2005; Borrello et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: Mutations at codon 634 of RET are found in approximately 84% of multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN2A) patients.
source: For example, mutations at codon 634 of RET are found in approximately 84% of multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN2A) patients (Santoro et al., 2004; de Graaff et al., 2001; Mulligan et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: Ret and Gdnf mRNA transcripts have been shown in mesenchymal cells of the second branchial arch in E9-9.5 mouse embryos.
source: Interestingly, Ret and Gdnf mRNA transcripts have been shown in mesenchymal cells of the second branchial arch in E9-9.5 mouse embryos (Golden et al., 1999; Natarajan et al., 2002), from which some facial muscles develop.
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: ret-gfrα3-artemin signalling is required to regulate myogenic differentiation in a subset of muscle precursors deriving from the first and second brachial arches in zebrafish.
source: We recently reported that ret is important for skeletal muscle development in zebrafish, where ret-gfrα3-artemin signalling is required to regulate myogenic differentiation in a subset of muscle precursors deriving from the first and second brachial arches (Knight et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to authors' own published work

claim: Ret51 was barely detectable in quiescent satellite cells.
source: Co-immunolabelling to detect Pax7 and Ret51 of fixed myofibres at T0 and T24 revealed that Ret51 was barely detectable in quiescent satellite cells, but expression increased after 24 hr of activation (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1A and B

claim: Ret51 expression increased after 24 hr of satellite cell activation.
source: Co-immunolabelling to detect Pax7 and Ret51 of fixed myofibres at T0 and T24 revealed that Ret51 was barely detectable in quiescent satellite cells, but expression increased after 24 hr of activation (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1A and B

claim: Phospho-Ret Tyr1062 immunolabelling increased after 24 hr of satellite cell activation, indicative of active Ret signalling.
source: This correlated with an increase in phospho-Ret Tyr1062 immunolabelling, indicative of active Ret signalling.
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data and inference about phosphorylation indicating activity

claim: Ret51 was found in both Myogenin-negative uncommitted myoblasts and Myogenin-positive differentiating myoblasts at T72.
source: By T72, a proportion of satellite cell-derived myoblasts stop expressing Pax7 and commit to myogenic differentiation, expressing Myogenin (Zammit et al., 2004). Ret51 was found in both Myogenin-negative uncommitted myoblasts and Myogenin-positive differentiating myoblasts (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Ret expression decreased during myoblast differentiation.
source: Expression of Ret decreased during myoblast differentiation, whereas Gfrα1, Gfrα2 and Gfrα4 increased upon differentiation.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data from satellite cell cultures

claim: Gfrα1, Gfrα2 and Gfrα4 expression increased upon myoblast differentiation.
source: Expression of Ret decreased during myoblast differentiation, whereas Gfrα1, Gfrα2 and Gfrα4 increased upon differentiation.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data from satellite cell cultures shown in Figure 1D-G

claim: Ret, Gfrα1, Gfrα2 and Gfrα4, but not Gfrα3, were robustly expressed in murine satellite cell-derived myoblast cultures.
source: Ret, Gfrα1, Gfrα2 and Gfrα4, but not Gfrα3, were robustly expressed in these myoblast cultures.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data from satellite cell cultures

claim: RET was detectable at low levels in proliferating and differentiating human primary myoblasts.
source: RNA was extracted from sister cultures for RT-qPCR analysis, which revealed that RET was detectable at low levels in proliferating and differentiating human primary myoblasts (Figure 2B)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Knockdown of Ret significantly reduced the proportion of myoblasts that had incorporated EdU from 44.0 ± 4.5% to 28.0 ± 3.2%.
source: Knockdown of Ret significantly reduced the proportion of myoblasts that had incorporated EdU, from a mean ± SEM of 44.0 ± 4.5% to 28.0 ± 3.2% (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Ret knockdown led to decreased proliferation, with significantly fewer cells in S and G1 phases.
source: Sister cultures of siRNA-treated myoblasts were then co-immunostained with phosphorylated-histone H1 and phosphorylated-histone H3 protein to identify specific stages of the cell cycle (Lu et al., 1994; Knopp et al., 2013; Hendzel et al., 1997). This confirmed that Ret knockdown led to decreased proliferation, with significantly fewer cells in S and G1 phases (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 3C

claim: siRNA-mediated knockdown of Ret was associated with a small decrease in the proportion of myoblasts containing Pax7 protein.
source: SiRNA-mediated knockdown of Ret was also associated with a small decrease in the proportion of myoblasts containing Pax7 protein (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Ret knockdown reduced Pax7 expression.
source: We also observed a reduction of Pax7 expression in response to Ret knockdown (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3E

claim: Ret knockdown did not alter MyoD or Myf5 expression.
source: Although Pax7 is genetically upstream of MyoD and Myf5 (Relaix et al., 2005), Ret knockdown did not alter MyoD (Figure 3F) or Myf5 expression (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3F and 3G

claim: The proportion of Myogenin-positive nuclei was significantly increased in Ret siRNA-treated cultures (85.4 ± 4.0%) relative to control siRNA-treated cells (69.1 ± 4.0%).
source: The proportion of Myogenin-positive nuclei was significantly increased in Ret siRNA-treated cultures relative to control siRNA-treated cells (85.4 ± 4.0% versus 69.1 ± 4.0%) (Figure 3J).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling quantification shown in Figure 3J

claim: The fusion index was unaltered in control cells (60.0 ± 3.0%) compared to cells treated with Ret siRNA (62.7 ± 2.2%).
source: In contrast, the proportion of nuclei in MyHC-expressing multinucleate myotubes (presented as the fusion index: the proportion of nuclei in myotubes of 2 or more nuclei, Figure 3K) was unaltered in control cells (60.0 ± 3.0%) compared to cells treated with Ret siRNA (62.7 ± 2.2%).
evidence: Supported by fusion index quantification shown in Figure 3K

claim: Ret siRNA knockdown led to more large myotubes (10.7 ± 1.9%) relative to control (5.4 ± 1.8%).
source: Ret siRNA knockdown led to more large myotubes (10.7 ± 1.9%) relative to control (5.4 ± 1.8%, Figure 3L).
evidence: Supported by myotube size quantification shown in Figure 3L

claim: Knockdown of Gfrα1, Gfrα2 and Gfrα4 were associated with fewer cells in the active stages of the cell cycle.
source: Phospho-Histone H1 and H3 immunostaining revealed that knockdown of Gfrα1, Gfrα2 and Gfrα4 were associated with fewer cells in the active stages of the cell cycle (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Knockdown of Gfrα4 was associated with fewer Pax7-containing satellite cell-derived myoblasts in proliferation medium, from 82.8 ± 2.0% in controls to 69.8 ± 4.3%.
source: As with Ret siRNA, knockdown of Gfrα4 (but not Gfrα1 or Gfrα2) was associated with fewer Pax7-containing satellite cell-derived myoblasts in proliferation medium, from 82.8 ± 2.0% in controls to 69.8 ± 4.3% in cells with siRNA to Gfrα4 (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by Pax7 quantification data shown in Figure 4B

claim: The proportion of Myogenin-positive nuclei was significantly increased following knockdown of Gfrα2 and Gfrα4.
source: After 48 hr in differentiation medium, the proportion of Myogenin-positive nuclei was significantly increased following knockdown of Gfrα2 and Gfrα4 (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by Myogenin quantification data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Knockdown of Gfrα4 significantly increased the fusion index from 39.3 ± 3.1% in the control sample to 46.8 ± 3.0%.
source: Additionally, knockdown of Gfrα4 significantly increased the fusion index (from 39.3 ± 3.1% in the control sample to 46.8 ± 3.0% with Gfrα4 siRNA (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by fusion index quantification shown in Figure 4D

claim: Retroviral constructs encoded RET protein of 170kDa as expected.
source: These retroviral constructs encoded RET protein of 170kDa as expected (Figure 5A)
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Human RET mRNA was present 48 hr after transduction of mouse myoblasts.
source: and human RET mRNA was present 48 hr after transduction of mouse myoblasts (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Expression of endogenous murine Ret was unaltered by human RET expression.
source: Expression of endogenous murine Ret was unaltered by human RET expression (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Constitutive expression of either wild-type RET9 or RET51 did not alter the proportion of eGFP+/EdU+ myoblasts compared to transduction with control retrovirus.
source: Constitutive expression of either wild-type RET9 or RET51 did not alter the proportion of eGFP+/EdU+ myoblasts compared to transduction with control retrovirus.
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation data

claim: CA RET constructs significantly increased proliferation rate, with EdU incorporation rising from 47.6 ± 0.8% in controls to 56.9 ± 1.8% (CA RET9) and 59.2 ± 1.7% (CA RET51).
source: However, the CA RET constructs significantly increased proliferation rate, with EdU incorporation rising from 47.6 ± 0.8% in controls to 56.9 ± 1.8% (CA RET9) and 59.2 ± 1.7% (CA RET51) (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 5D and E

claim: RET did not alter the overall proportion of Pax7-containing cells.
source: RET did not alter the overall proportion of Pax7-containing cells (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: Supported by Pax7 quantification data shown in Figure 5F and G

claim: After 24 hr of differentiation, CA RET51 reduced the proportion of myoblasts that contained Myogenin (49.5 ± 1.2%) relative to controls (58.9 ± 3.1%).
source: After 24 hr of differentiation, CA RET51 reduced the proportion of myoblasts that contained Myogenin (49.5 ± 1.2%) relative to controls (58.9 ± 3.1%), but by 48 hr there was no longer any difference (Figure 5H and I).
evidence: Supported by Myogenin quantification data shown in Figure 5H and I

claim: At 48 hr of differentiation, there was no alteration in fusion index with CA RET51 expression.
source: At this stage, there was no alteration in fusion index (Figure 5J and K).
evidence: Supported by fusion index data shown in Figure 5J and K

claim: Ret expression was increased 3.45-fold in DUX4-expressing satellite cell-derived myoblasts.
source: Ret expression was increased 3.45-fold in DUX4-expressing satellite cell-derived myoblasts, and approximately 2 fold by either tMALDUX4-VP16 or tMALDUX4-ERD, relative to controls.
evidence: Supported by microarray data analysis

claim: Expression of Ret co-receptors Gfrα2, Gfrα3 and Gfrα4 were unaltered by DUX4.
source: Expression of Ret co-receptors Gfrα2, Gfrα3 and Gfrα4 were unaltered, although Gfrα1 expression was reduced 0.57-fold by DUX4 (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by microarray data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Gfrα1 expression was reduced 0.57-fold by DUX4.
source: Expression of Ret co-receptors Gfrα2, Gfrα3 and Gfrα4 were unaltered, although Gfrα1 expression was reduced 0.57-fold by DUX4 (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by microarray data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Expression of DUX4c did not alter Ret or Gfrα co-receptor expression.
source: Expression of DUX4c did not alter Ret or Gfrα co-receptor expression (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by microarray data shown in Figure 6A

claim: DUX4 significantly increased total Ret expression (97.5-fold) after 48 hr relative to control plasmid-transduced cells.
source: There was a trend for DUX4 to increase Ret transcription after 24 hr (p=0.052), which increased significantly (97.5-fold) after 48 hr, relative to control plasmid-transduced cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6B

claim: DUX4 increased expression of Ret9 (150-fold) more than Ret51 (15.8-fold) after 48 hr.
source: Using isoform-specific primers, we found that DUX4 increased expression of Ret9 (150-fold) more than Ret51 (15.8-fold) after 48 hr (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6C and D

claim: Expression of Ret was significantly increased after 12 hr of DUX4 induction in iC2C12-DUX4 cells and maintained at elevated levels at 24 and 48 hr.
source: Using inducible iC2C12-DUX4 and iC2C12-DUX4c myoblasts (Dandapat et al., 2013), expression of Ret was significantly increased after 12 hr of induction with 200ng/ml doxycycline in the iC2C12-DUX4 line, compared to un-induced myoblasts, and maintained at elevated levels at 24 and 48 hr of induction (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6E

claim: Induction of DUX4c in the iC2C12-DUX4c line did not generally alter Ret expression.
source: Induction of DUX4c in the iC2C12-DUX4c line did not generally alter Ret expression (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6F

claim: DUX4 activation of Ret led to the detection of membrane-located Ret protein.
source: DUX4 activation of Ret also led to the detection of membrane-located Ret protein, as revealed by immunolabelling with an antibody to Ret51 in DUX4-infected myoblasts (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 6G

claim: Over-expression of either RET isoform significantly reduced caspase 3/7 release.
source: However, over-expression of either RET isoform significantly reduced caspase 3/7 release, implying that DUX4-mediated up-regulation of RET does not contribute to the apoptotic phenotype (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by caspase 3/7 assay data shown in Figure 7B

claim: DUX4-mediated up-regulation of RET does not contribute to the apoptotic phenotype.
source: However, over-expression of either RET isoform significantly reduced caspase 3/7 release, implying that DUX4-mediated up-regulation of RET does not contribute to the apoptotic phenotype (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by caspase 3/7 assay data and inference from the results

claim: Transfection of Ret siRNA into DUX4-expressing cells did not significantly alter the proportion of cells incorporating EdU relative to control siRNA treated cells.
source: Transfection of Ret siRNA into DUX4-expressing cells did not significantly alter the proportion of cells incorporating EdU relative to control siRNA treated cells.
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation data

claim: Knockdown of Ret did not rescue the reduced number of eGFP+/Pax7+ myoblasts in the presence of DUX4.
source: Knockdown of Ret did not rescue the reduced number of eGFP+/Pax7+ myoblasts in the presence of DUX4 (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by Pax7 quantification data shown in Figure 7D

claim: Ret knockdown is unable to rescue the DUX4-mediated proliferation defect in murine primary myoblasts.
source: Together, this suggests that Ret knockdown is unable to rescue the DUX4-mediated proliferation defect in murine primary myoblasts.
evidence: Inferred from EdU and Pax7 data showing no rescue

claim: There was a slight increase in the fusion index of myoblasts expressing control retrovirus and transfected with siRNA against Ret relative to control siRNA (p=3.06 × 10–4).
source: There was a slight increase in the fusion index of myoblasts expressing control retrovirus and transfected with siRNA against Ret relative to control siRNA (p=3.06 × 10–4, Figure 7E, F and G, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fusion index data shown in Figure 7E, F and G

claim: Myoblasts expressing DUX4 (GFP+) had a dramatically reduced fusion index when transfected with control siRNA (p=2.71 × 10–65).
source: Myoblasts expressing DUX4 (GFP+) had a dramatically reduced fusion index when transfected with control siRNA (p=2.71 × 10–65).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fusion index data

claim: Ret knockdown rescued myoblast fusion in the presence of DUX4, relative to cells expressing DUX4 and transfected with a control siRNA (p=2.15 × 10–21).
source: In contrast, Ret knockdown rescued myoblast fusion in the presence of DUX4, relative to cells expressing DUX4 and transfected with a control siRNA (p=2.15 × 10–21).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fusion index data

claim: Ret knockdown significantly improves myogenic differentiation in the presence of DUX4.
source: Therefore, Ret knockdown significantly improves myogenic differentiation in the presence of DUX4.
evidence: Inferred from fusion rescue data

claim: All three RTK inhibitors (Sunitinib, TG101209, Zactima) significantly rescued muscle differentiation in CA RET51-expressing C2C12s.

source: ERK1/2 phosphorylation was inhibited by Sunitinib in DUX4-expressing iC2C12-DUX4 myoblasts, but not in control myoblasts not expressing DUX4, suggesting a potential mechanism by which DUX4-mediated Ret signalling could inhibit differentiation.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data and inference about mechanism

claim: AKT phosphorylation was unaltered by inducing DUX4.
source: In contrast, AKT phosphorylation was unaltered by inducing DUX4.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data

claim: It is possible that Sunitinib could also be acting on ERK1/2 phosphorylation activated by other pathways perturbed by, or in response to, DUX4.
source: Although Ret can operate through ERK1/2 signalling, it is possible that Sunitinib could also be acting on ERK1/2 phosphorylation activated by other pathways perturbed by, or in response to, DUX4.
evidence: Speculation about alternative mechanisms

claim: Sunitinib could induce the FSHD myoblasts to adopt the phenotype of isogenic myoblasts lacking the D4Z4 contraction.
source: Using statistical models we showed that Sunitinib could induce the FSHD myoblasts to adopt the phenotype of isogenic myoblasts lacking the D4Z4 contraction.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of morphology, proliferation and differentiation data

claim: Increased engraftment of FSHD myoblasts occurred in response to daily systemic Sunitinib treatment in transplantation assays.
source: Transplantation assays of FSHD myoblasts into cryodamaged immunodeficient mice showed increased engraftment of FSHD myoblasts occurred in response to daily systemic Sunitinib treatment.
evidence: Supported by in vivo transplantation data

claim: This pre-clinical model identifies Sunitinib as a potential therapeutic agent for FSHD.
source: Therefore, this pre-clinical model for evaluating modifiers of FSHD pathology identifies Sunitinib as a potential therapeutic agent for FSHD.
evidence: Inferred from in vitro and in vivo rescue data

claim: Ret is a novel regulator of satellite cell function in mammalian muscle.
source: In conclusion, we have shown that Ret is a novel regulator of satellite cell function in mammalian muscle, and contributes to the FSHD phenotype.
evidence: Inferred from all experimental data showing Ret's role in satellite cells

claim: Blocking DUX4-mediated Ret signalling increases myogenic differentiation.
source: Specifically, blocking DUX4-mediated Ret signalling increases myogenic differentiation, giving further insight into the molecular pathology of DUX4 and highlighting Ret signalling as potential drug target.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments with siRNA and Sunitinib

claim: The clinically-approved RET inhibitor Sunitinib rescues cell morphology, proliferation and myogenic differentiation in human FSHD myoblasts both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Crucially, the clinically-approved RET inhibitor Sunitinib (Widmer et al., 2014) rescues cell morphology, proliferation and myogenic differentiation in human FSHD myoblasts both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: Supported by in vitro and in vivo experimental data with human FSHD cells

claim: RTK inhibitors are a potential novel therapeutic strategy to treat muscle wasting in FSHD.
source: Given that FSHD is currently incurable, our findings highlight RTK inhibitors as a potential novel therapeutic strategy to treat muscle wasting in FSHD.
evidence: Inferred from all rescue data with Sunitinib
